questions.question: Which of the following pairs have DIFFERENT expressive power?

options.A: Deterministic finite automata (DFA) and Non-deterministic finite automata (NFA)
options.B:
Deterministic push down automata (DPDA) and Non-deterministic push down
automata (NPDA)
options.C:
Deterministic single-tape Turing machine and Non-deterministic single tape
Turing machine
options.D: Single-tape Turing machine and multi-tape Turing machine

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- DFA = NFA (subset construction)
- Deterministic TM = non-deterministic TM, and single-tape TM = multi-tape TM
- DPDA accept only deterministic CFLs. NPDA accept all CFLs (e.g. [latex]ww^R[/latex] needs non-determinism)

Answer: DPDA and NPDA

questions.question: Suppose that [latex]L_1[/latex] is a regular language and [latex]L_2[/latex] is a context-free language. Which one of the following languages is NOT necessarily context-free?
questions.explanation:
With [latex]L_1[/latex] regular and [latex]L_2[/latex] CFL:
- [latex]L_1\cap L_2[/latex], [latex]L_1\cdot L_2[/latex], [latex]L_1\cup L_2[/latex] are always CFL (closure properties).
- [latex]L_1-L_2=L_1\cap\overline{L_2}[/latex] needs the complement of a CFL, which need not be CFL. E.g. [latex]L_1=\Sigma^*[/latex] gives just [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex].

Answer: [latex]L_1-L_2[/latex]

questions.question:
Which one of the following statements is equivalent to the following assertion?

Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] decides the language [latex]L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*[/latex]

options.A: Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] halts on all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}[/latex]
options.B: Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] accepts all input strings in [latex]L[/latex]
options.C: Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] rejects all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}-L[/latex]
options.D: Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] accepts all input strings in [latex]L[/latex] and rejects all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}-L[/latex]

questions.explanation:
A Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] "decides" a language [latex]L[/latex] means [latex]M[/latex] is a total decider for [latex]L[/latex]: it must halt on every input, and its halting outcome must correctly classify membership — accepting every string that is in [latex]L[/latex], and rejecting every string that is not in [latex]L[/latex] (i.e. every string in [latex]\{0,1\}^*-L[/latex]).

Simply halting on all inputs (without specifying correct accept/reject behavior) isn't enough by itself, and neither "accepts all of [latex]L[/latex]" nor "rejects all of the complement" alone captures the full requirement (each addresses only one direction). Only the combination of both conditions together is equivalent to "decides [latex]L[/latex]."

Answer: M accepts all strings in L and rejects all strings in {0,1}*-L

questions.question: Let [latex]\Sigma[/latex] be a finite non-empty alphabet and let [latex]2^{\Sigma^{*}}[/latex] be the power set of [latex]\Sigma^{*}[/latex] . Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.explanation:
[latex]\Sigma^*[/latex] can be listed in order of length (then dictionary order), so it is countably infinite.

[latex]2^{\Sigma^*}[/latex] is the power set of a countably infinite set, which is uncountable (Cantor's theorem).

Answer: [latex]2^{\Sigma^*}[/latex] is uncountable and [latex]\Sigma^*[/latex] is countable

questions.question: Which one of the following regular expressions is equivalent to the language accepted by the DFA given below?
questions.explanation:
The start state loops on 0 and goes to the final state on 1; the final state loops on 0 and returns on 1. So the DFA accepts strings with an odd number of 1s.

[latex]0^*1(0+10^*1)^*[/latex]: [latex]0^*[/latex] stays at start, [latex]1[/latex] reaches the final state, then [latex]0[/latex] (self-loop) or [latex]10^*1[/latex] (go back and return) keeps it final. This is exactly "odd number of 1s".

Others fail on "1" (odd, accepted): [latex]0^*(10^*11)^*0^*[/latex], [latex]0^*1(010^*1)^*0^*[/latex] cannot give "111", and [latex]0(1+0^*10^*1)^*0^*[/latex] must start with 0.

Answer: [latex]0^*1(0+10^*1)^*[/latex]

questions.question: Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.B: The language L = {[latex]a^{n}[/latex]| n is prime} is regular
options.C: The language L={ w | w has 3k +1    b's for some k [latex]\in[/latex] N with [latex]\Sigma[/latex] = {a,b} } is regular.
options.D: The language L = { ww| w[latex]\in \Sigma^{*}[/latex] with [latex]\Sigma[/latex]={0,1}} is regular.

questions.explanation:
Counting b's modulo 3 needs only 3 states, so "number of b's is 3k + 1" is regular. [latex]a^nb^n[/latex], prime-length strings and ww all need unbounded memory, so they are not regular.

Answer: The language with 3k+1 b's is regular

questions.question: Which one of the following regular expressions represents the language: the set of all binary strings having two consecutive 0s and two consecutive 1s?

The string must contain "00" somewhere and "11" somewhere, in either order:
[latex](0+1)^*\big(00(0+1)^*11+11(0+1)^*00\big)(0+1)^*[/latex] True

- Option 3 needs only one of them.

questions.question: Let N be an NFA with n states. Let k be the number of states of a minimal DFA which is equivalent to N. Which one of the following is necessarily true?
questions.explanation:
The subset construction turns an n-state NFA into a DFA whose states are subsets of the NFA's states, at most [latex]2^n[/latex]. The minimal DFA cannot be bigger, but it can be much smaller (so the other bounds are not guaranteed).

Answer: [latex]k\le2^n[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider the following expression grammar G:
E[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]E-T|T
T[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]T+F|F
F[latex]\rightarrow[/latex](E)|id
Which of the following grammars is not left recursive, but is equivalent to G?
questions.explanation:
Remove left recursion with the standard rule [latex]A\rightarrow A\alpha\mid\beta\Rightarrow A\rightarrow\beta A',\ A'\rightarrow\alpha A'\mid\epsilon[/latex]:
- [latex]E\rightarrow E-T\mid T[/latex] becomes [latex]E\rightarrow TX,\ X\rightarrow-TX\mid\epsilon[/latex]
- [latex]T\rightarrow T+F\mid F[/latex] becomes [latex]T\rightarrow FY,\ Y\rightarrow+FY\mid\epsilon[/latex]

Option 1 is still left recursive, option 2 keeps [latex]T\rightarrow T+F[/latex] and loses the minus, option 4 changes the language.

Answer: Option 3

questions.question:
Consider the following language.

L={[latex]x \in \{a,b\}^*|[/latex] number of a's in x divisible by 2 but not divisible by 3}

The minimum number of states in DFA that accepts L is _______
questions.explanation:
The DFA must track (number of a's) mod 2 and mod 3, i.e. mod 6: 6 states (b's do not change state).

Accept counts that are even but not multiples of 3: remainders 2 and 4. All 6 states are distinguishable (e.g. they differ in how many a's lead to acceptance).

Answer: 6

questions.question:
Consider the context-free grammar [latex]G[/latex] below
[latex] S\rightarrow aSb \;| \;X[/latex]
[latex] X\rightarrow aX \;| \;Xb \;|\; a\;|\; b[/latex]
where [latex]S[/latex] and [latex]X[/latex] are non-terminals, and [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are terminal symbols. The starting non-terminal is [latex]S[/latex].
Which one of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: The language generated by [latex] G \text{ is }(a + b)^*[/latex]
options.B: The language generated by [latex] G \text{ is } a^*(a + b)b^*[/latex]
options.C: The language generated by [latex] G \text{ is }a^*b^*(a + b)[/latex]
options.D: The language generated by [latex] G[/latex] is not a regular language

questions.explanation:
X: [latex]X\rightarrow aX[/latex] adds a's on the left, [latex]X\rightarrow Xb[/latex] adds b's on the right, ending with a or b. So [latex]L(X)=a^*(a+b)b^*[/latex].

[latex]S\rightarrow aSb[/latex] only adds more a's on the left and more b's on the right of X, so the result stays in [latex]a^*(a+b)b^*[/latex] and covers all of it (use S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] X directly).

This is regular, and it is not [latex](a+b)^*[/latex] (e.g. "ba" is missing).

Answer: The language generated by G is [latex]a^*(a+b)b^*[/latex]

questions.question:
Which of the following is/are undecidable?
1. G is a CFG. Is L(G) = [latex]\Phi[/latex]?
2. G is a CFG. Is L(G) = [latex]\Sigma ^{*}[/latex] ?
3. M is a Turing machine. Is L(M) regular?
4. A is a DFA and N is an NFA. Is L(A) = L(N)?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- 1: emptiness of a CFG is decidable
- 2: whether L(G) = [latex]\Sigma^*[/latex] for a CFG is undecidable
- 3: regularity of L(M) for a TM is undecidable (Rice's theorem)
- 4: equivalence of a DFA and an NFA is decidable (convert and minimise)

Answer: 2 and 3 only

questions.question:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet [latex]\{a, b, c\}[/latex], where [latex]m[/latex] and [latex]n[/latex] are natural numbers:

[latex]L_1 = \{ a^m b^m c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1 \}[/latex]
[latex]L_2 = \{ a^m b^n c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1 \}[/latex]

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.B: [latex]L_1[/latex] is a context-free language but [latex]L_2[/latex] is not a context-free language.
options.C: [latex]L_1[/latex] is not a context-free language but [latex]L_2[/latex] is a context-free language.

questions.explanation:
[latex]L_1=\{a^mb^mc^{m+n}\mid m,n\ge1\}[/latex]: this requires two separate comparisons tied to the same value [latex]m[/latex] — matching [latex]a[/latex]'s against [latex]b[/latex]'s exactly (using up a stack), and independently comparing the [latex]c[/latex]-count against that same [latex]m[/latex] again. A single-stack PDA can only "remember and compare" one running count at a time; once the stack is used up matching [latex]a[/latex]'s against [latex]b[/latex]'s, the value of [latex]m[/latex] is no longer available to compare against the [latex]c[/latex]'s. This mirrors the classic non-context-free pattern [latex]a^nb^nc^n[/latex]. [latex]L_1[/latex] is not context-free.

[latex]L_2=\{a^mb^nc^{m+n}\mid m,n\ge1\}[/latex]: here the [latex]c[/latex]-count only needs to match the combined total of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s (not two separate comparisons). A single stack handles this easily: push one symbol for every [latex]a[/latex] and every [latex]b[/latex] (treating them the same way), then pop one symbol per [latex]c[/latex], accepting if the stack empties exactly when the input ends. [latex]L_2[/latex] is context-free.

Answer: L1 is not context-free but L2 is context-free.

Click here for detail solution

questions.question:
For a Turing machine M, < M > denotes an encoding of M. Consider the following two languages.

[latex]\begin{array}{ll} L1 = \{ \langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ takes more than } 2021 \text{ steps on all inputs} \} \\ L2 = \{ \langle M \rangle \mid M\text{ takes more than } 2021 \text{ steps on some input} \} \end{array}[/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: Both L1 and L2 are decidable.
options.B: L1 is decidable  and L2 is undecidable.
options.C: L1 is undecidable  and L2 is decidable.
options.D: Both L1 and L2 are undecidable.

questions.explanation:
In 2021 steps, M can read at most the first 2021 input symbols. So "more than 2021 steps" depends only on inputs of length up to 2021, a finite set.

Simulate M for 2022 steps on each such input; this decides both "on all inputs" (L1) and "on some input" (L2).

Answer: Both L1 and L2 are decidable
